claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is the causative agent of tuberculosis.
source: Diverse chemical modifications fine-tune the function and metabolism of tRNA. Although tRNA modification is universal in all kingdoms of life, profiles of modifications, their functions, and physiological roles have not been elucidated in most organisms including the human pathogen, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established knowledge about Mtb.

claim: tRNA modification is universal in all kingdoms of life.
source: Although tRNA modification is universal in all kingdoms of life, profiles of modifications, their functions, and physiological roles have not been elucidated in most organisms including the human pathogen, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Profiles of tRNA modifications, their functions, and physiological roles have not been elucidated in most organisms including Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: Although tRNA modification is universal in all kingdoms of life, profiles of modifications, their functions, and physiological roles have not been elucidated in most organisms including the human pathogen, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field, providing context for the study.

claim: Homology searches identified 23 candidate tRNA modifying enzymes in Mtb that are predicted to create 16 tRNA modifications across all tRNA species.
source: Homology searches identified 23 candidate tRNA modifying enzymes that are predicted to create 16 tRNA modifications across all tRNA species.
evidence: This is a direct result from the homology search analysis performed in the study.

claim: Reverse transcription-derived error signatures in tRNA-seq predicted the sites and presence of nine modifications.
source: Reverse transcription-derived error signatures in tRNA-seq predicted the sites and presence of nine modifications.
evidence: This is a finding from the tRNA-seq experiments conducted in the study.

claim: Several chemical treatments prior to tRNA-seq expanded the number of predictable modifications.
source: Several chemical treatments prior to tRNA-seq expanded the number of predictable modifications.
evidence: This is a methodological finding from the study showing that chemical treatments enhance detection.

claim: Deletion of Mtb genes encoding TruB and MnmA eliminated their respective tRNA modifications.
source: Deletion of Mtb genes encoding two modifying enzymes, TruB and MnmA, eliminated their respective tRNA modifications, validating the presence of modified sites in tRNA species.
evidence: This is an experimental result from gene deletion studies validating the function of these enzymes.

claim: The absence of mnmA attenuated Mtb growth in macrophages.
source: Furthermore, the absence of mnmA attenuated Mtb growth in macrophages, suggesting that MnmA-dependent tRNA uridine sulfation contributes to Mtb intracellular growth.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from macrophage infection assays.

claim: MnmA-dependent tRNA uridine sulfation contributes to Mtb intracellular growth.
source: Furthermore, the absence of mnmA attenuated Mtb growth in macrophages, suggesting that MnmA-dependent tRNA uridine sulfation contributes to Mtb intracellular growth.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from the mnmA deletion mutant growth assay.

claim: tRNA is an adaptor molecule that enables protein synthesis by converting the triplet genetic code in mRNA into amino acids.
source: tRNA is an adaptor molecule that enables protein synthesis by converting the triplet genetic code in mRNA into amino acids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the fundamental role of tRNA in translation.

claim: The fidelity of base pairing between mRNA codons and tRNA anticodons is monitored within ribosomes and is critical for properly incorporating amino acids into growing polypeptides.
source: The fidelity of base pairing between mRNA codons and tRNA anticodons is monitored within ribosomes and is critical for properly incorporating the amino acids bound to the 3′ ends of tRNAs into growing polypeptides.
evidence: This is established knowledge about translation fidelity.

claim: The abundances and properties of tRNA isoacceptors are fine tuned by diverse mechanisms, including chemical modifications.
source: For optimal translation, the abundances, and properties of tRNA isoacceptors are fine tuned by diverse mechanisms, including chemical modifications (Huang and Hopper, 2016; Björk and Hagervall, 2014; Shepherd and Ibba, 2015; Torrent et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Dysregulation of tRNA abundance and/or structure leads to defective decoding and results in ribosome pausing and collisions, protein misfolding, stress responses and can have detrimental or lethal effects on the cell.
source: Dysregulation of tRNA abundance and/or structure leads to defective decoding and results in ribosome pausing and collisions, protein misfolding, stress responses and can have detrimental or lethal effects on the cell (Orellana et al., 2022; Suzuki, 2021; Liu et al., 2022; Goodarzi et al., 2016; Delaunay et al., 2022; Nedialkova and Leidel, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Chemical modifications of tRNA are found in all kingdoms of life.
source: Chemical modifications of tRNA (tRNA modifications) are found in all kingdoms of life and fine-tune tRNA properties including mRNA decoding efficiency, recognition by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, half-life, and structural stability (Björk and Hagervall, 2014; Nedialkova and Leidel, 2015; Kimura and Waldor, 2019; Giegé and Eriani, 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: tRNA modifications fine-tune tRNA properties including mRNA decoding efficiency, recognition by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, half-life, and structural stability.
source: Chemical modifications of tRNA (tRNA modifications) are found in all kingdoms of life and fine-tune tRNA properties including mRNA decoding efficiency, recognition by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, half-life, and structural stability (Björk and Hagervall, 2014; Nedialkova and Leidel, 2015; Kimura and Waldor, 2019; Giegé and Eriani, 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Modifications are prevalent in the anticodon loop, particularly at the first letter of the anticodon.
source: Modifications are prevalent in the anticodon loop, particularly at the first letter of the anticodon.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tRNA modification patterns.

claim: Modifications of the anticodon loop directly modulate codon recognition.
source: Modifications of the anticodon loop directly modulate codon recognition, whereas modifications in the tRNA body region primarily stabilize tRNA tertiary structure, protecting them from degradation in the cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the functional roles of tRNA modifications in different regions.

claim: Modifications in the tRNA body region primarily stabilize tRNA tertiary structure, protecting them from degradation in the cell.
source: Modifications of the anticodon loop directly modulate codon recognition, whereas modifications in the tRNA body region primarily stabilize tRNA tertiary structure, protecting them from degradation in the cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the functional roles of tRNA modifications in different regions.

claim: tRNA modifications are generated by dedicated site-specific enzymes referred to as tRNA modifying enzymes.
source: tRNA modifications are generated by dedicated site-specific enzymes referred to as tRNA modifying enzymes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about how tRNA modifications are synthesized.

claim: tRNA modifications have been extensively characterized in a few model organisms.
source: tRNA modifications have been extensively characterized in a few model organisms (Björk and Hagervall, 2014; de Crécy-Lagard and Jaroch, 2021), but their profiles, regulation, and functions in non-model organisms, including bacterial pathogens, are understudied (de Crécy-Lagard and Jaroch, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The profiles, regulation, and functions of tRNA modifications in non-model organisms, including bacterial pathogens, are understudied.
source: tRNA modifications have been extensively characterized in a few model organisms (Björk and Hagervall, 2014; de Crécy-Lagard and Jaroch, 2021), but their profiles, regulation, and functions in non-model organisms, including bacterial pathogens, are understudied (de Crécy-Lagard and Jaroch, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: tRNA sequencing (tRNA-seq) allows for the rapid and systematic prediction of many tRNA modification sites.
source: tRNA sequencing (tRNA-seq) allows for the rapid and systematic prediction of many tRNA modification sites (Zhang et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A comparative tRNA-seq protocol was developed to profile tRNA modifications in Vibrio cholerae, leading to the discovery of a new RNA modification and RNA editing process.
source: We recently developed a comparative tRNA-seq protocol to profile tRNA modifications in organisms with uncharted tRNA modification profiles; in Vibrio cholerae, this approach led to the discovery of a new RNA modification and RNA editing process (Kimura et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: tRNA-seq enables rapid prediction of modified sites through detection of reverse transcription-derived signatures, such as nucleotide misincorporation and early termination.
source: tRNA-seq enables rapid prediction of modified sites through detection of reverse transcription-derived signatures, such as nucleotide misincorporation and early termination, both of which occur more frequently at modified sites.
evidence: This describes the methodological principle of tRNA-seq based on established knowledge.

claim: Nucleotide misincorporation and early termination occur more frequently at modified sites during reverse transcription.
source: tRNA-seq enables rapid prediction of modified sites through detection of reverse transcription-derived signatures, such as nucleotide misincorporation and early termination, both of which occur more frequently at modified sites.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the behavior of reverse transcriptase at modified sites.

claim: Several chemical treatments of tRNA can convert modifications that are not recognizable as reverse transcription-derived signatures into detectable signals, expanding the repertoire of modifications that can be distinguished by tRNA-seq.
source: Furthermore, several chemical treatments of tRNA can convert modifications that are not recognizable as reverse transcription-derived signatures into detectable signals, expanding the repertoire of modifications that can be distinguished by tRNA-seq (Motorin and Helm, 2019; Finet et al., 2022; Draycott et al., 2022; Dai et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) caused >10.5 million cases and over 1.5 million deaths worldwide in 2020.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the agent of tuberculosis (TB), is a global pathogen that caused >10.5 million cases and over 1.5 million deaths worldwide in 2020 (W.H.O, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a WHO report.

claim: Several studies have uncovered roles for non-Mtb mycobacterial tRNA modifications in stress responses, adaptation to environmental changes, and persister cell formation.
source: Several studies have uncovered roles for non-Mtb mycobacterial tRNA modifications in stress responses, adaptation to environmental changes, and persister cell formation (Chionh et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Mycobacterium bovis BCG responds to hypoxia by reprogramming 40 ribonucleoside modifications in tRNA to facilitate translation of a subset of proteins that promote survival in hypoxic conditions.
source: Mycobacterium bovis BCG, an organism closely related to Mtb, responds to hypoxia by reprogramming 40 ribonucleoside modifications in tRNA to facilitate translation of a subset of proteins that promote survival in hypoxic conditions (Chionh et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Studies of the profiles and functions of Mtb tRNA modifications have been limited to date.
source: To date, studies of the profiles and functions of Mtb tRNA modifications have been limited.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: With a stringent threshold (E-value <1 × 10−10), 31 Mtb genes homologous to genes encoding known RNA modification enzymes were identified.
source: With a stringent threshold (E-value <1 × 10−10), 31 Mtb genes homologous to genes encoding known RNA modification enzymes were identified (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct result from the BLAST homology search analysis.

claim: Twenty-three of the identified genes are predicted to synthesize 16 tRNA modifications in Mtb.
source: Twenty-three of these genes are predicted to synthesize 16 tRNA modifications in Mtb (Supplementary files 2 and 3), including miaA and miaB for 2-methylthio-6-isopentenyl-adenosine (ms2i6A), tsaD, tsaB, tsaE, and sua5 for N6-threonylcarbamoyladenosine (t6A), mnmA for 2-thiouridine (s2U), truB, truA, rluA, and pus9 for pseudouridine (Ψ), trm2 for 5-methyluridine (m5U), trmD for 1-methylguanosine (m1G), trmI for 1-methyladenosine (m1A), trmL for 2′-O-methylcytidine (Cm) or 2′-O-methyluridine (Um), trmB for 7-methylguanosine (m7G), two trmH for 2′-O-methylguanosine (Gm), trmR for 5-methoxyuridine (mo5U), trcM for 5-methylcytidine (m5C), dusB for dihydrouridine (D), tadA for inosine (I), and tilS for lysidine (k2C).
evidence: This is a prediction based on homology search results.

claim: Five genes encoding Mtb tRNA modifying enzymes (trmD, tilS, tadA, tsaC2, and miaA) were reported to be essential for Mtb growth in both Tn-seq and CRISPRi screens.
source: Five genes encoding Mtb tRNA modifying enzymes, trmD, tilS, tadA, tsaC2, and miaA, were reported to be essential for Mtb growth in both Tn-seq (DeJesus et al., 2017) and CRISPRi screens (Bosch et al., 2021; Supplementary file 3), suggesting that the modifications they produce are critical for tRNA functions.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior Tn-seq and CRISPRi screen data.

claim: The modifications produced by trmD, tilS, tadA, tsaC2, and miaA are critical for tRNA functions.
source: Five genes encoding Mtb tRNA modifying enzymes, trmD, tilS, tadA, tsaC2, and miaA, were reported to be essential for Mtb growth in both Tn-seq (DeJesus et al., 2017) and CRISPRi screens (Bosch et al., 2021; Supplementary file 3), suggesting that the modifications they produce are critical for tRNA functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the essentiality of these genes in genetic screens.

claim: E. coli trmD, tilS, tadA, and tsaC2 are essential for growth and critical for codon decoding, aminoacylation, and reading frame maintenance.
source: Indeed, E. coli trmD, tilS, tadA, and tsaC2 are also essential for growth and critical for codon decoding, aminoacylation, and reading frame maintenance (Masuda et al., 2022; Soma et al., 2003; Wolf et al., 2002; El Yacoubi et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature on E. coli.

claim: The Mtb modifications synthesized by trmD, tilS, tadA, and tsaC2 likely have similar impacts on tRNA functions as in E. coli.
source: The Mtb modifications synthesized by these enzymes likely have similar impacts on tRNA functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of these enzymes and their functions in E. coli.

claim: MiaA is non-essential in E. coli grown in nutrient-rich medium.
source: Unexpectedly, one modifying enzyme, MiaA, is non-essential in E. coli grown in nutrient-rich medium, but apparently essential in Mtb, suggesting that i6A, the modification introduced by MiaA, may have more profound roles in Mtb translation than in E. coli.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli MiaA.

claim: MiaA is apparently essential in Mtb.
source: Unexpectedly, one modifying enzyme, MiaA, is non-essential in E. coli grown in nutrient-rich medium, but apparently essential in Mtb, suggesting that i6A, the modification introduced by MiaA, may have more profound roles in Mtb translation than in E. coli.
evidence: This is based on the Tn-seq and CRISPRi screen data showing miaA is essential in Mtb.

claim: i6A, the modification introduced by MiaA, may have more profound roles in Mtb translation than in E. coli.
source: Unexpectedly, one modifying enzyme, MiaA, is non-essential in E. coli grown in nutrient-rich medium, but apparently essential in Mtb, suggesting that i6A, the modification introduced by MiaA, may have more profound roles in Mtb translation than in E. coli.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the differential essentiality of MiaA in E. coli versus Mtb.

claim: Several of the putative Mtb tRNA modifying enzymes are conserved across all three domains of life (e.g., TruB and TsaD).
source: Several of the putative Mtb tRNA modifying enzymes are conserved across all three domains of life (e.g., TruB and TsaD) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Some tRNA modifying enzymes were limited to bacterial species closely related to Mtb, possibly suggesting their species-specific physiological roles, including pathogenesis.
source: By contrast, some enzymes were limited to bacterial species closely related to Mtb, possibly suggesting their species-specific physiological roles, including pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the phylogenetic distribution of certain enzymes.

claim: TrmI (Rv2118c) homologs are widely present in Archaea and Eukaryotes, but are sparsely distributed in bacteria, where they are primarily limited to Actinomycetia, including Mtb, and several thermophilic bacterial species.
source: For example, TrmI (Rv2118c) homologs are widely present in Archaea and Eukaryotes, but are sparsely distributed in bacteria, where they are primarily limited to Actinomycetia, including Mtb, and several thermophilic bacterial species (e.g., Thermus thermophilus).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis of TrmI homologs.

claim: TrmI synthesizes m1A at position 58 in eukaryotes.
source: TrmI synthesizes m1A at position 58 in eukaryotes (Anderson et al., 1998) and at position 57/58 in archaea (Guelorget et al., 2010); indeed, TrmI in Mtb has been proven to generate m1A at position 58 (Varshney et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: TrmI synthesizes m1A at position 57/58 in archaea.
source: TrmI synthesizes m1A at position 58 in eukaryotes (Anderson et al., 1998) and at position 57/58 in archaea (Guelorget et al., 2010); indeed, TrmI in Mtb has been proven to generate m1A at position 58 (Varshney et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: TrmI in Mtb has been proven to generate m1A at position 58.
source: TrmI synthesizes m1A at position 58 in eukaryotes (Anderson et al., 1998) and at position 57/58 in archaea (Guelorget et al., 2010); indeed, TrmI in Mtb has been proven to generate m1A at position 58 (Varshney et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Pus9 (Rv3300c) has many homologs exhibiting weak similarity across eukaryotes and bacteria.
source: Pus9 (Rv3300c) has many homologs exhibiting weak similarity across eukaryotes and bacteria.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis of Pus9 homologs.

claim: Some species, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and several species of Actinomycetia, encode proteins showing strong homology to Mtb Pus9.
source: However, some species, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and several species of Actinomycetia, encode proteins showing strong homology to Mtb Pus9, suggesting that this set of pseudouridylases have a distinctive property such as substrate specificity.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis of Pus9 homologs.

claim: The set of pseudouridylases showing strong homology to Mtb Pus9 may have a distinctive property such as substrate specificity.
source: However, some species, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and several species of Actinomycetia, encode proteins showing strong homology to Mtb Pus9, suggesting that this set of pseudouridylases have a distinctive property such as substrate specificity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the phylogenetic distribution pattern.

claim: tRNA modifying enzymes predicted in Mtb were observed in mycobacteria species, including Mycolicibacterium smegmatis and Mycobacteroides abscessus.
source: tRNA modifying enzymes predicted in Mtb were observed in mycobacteria species, including Mycolicibacterium smegmatis and Mycobacteroides abscessus (Figure 1), suggesting that tRNA modification patterns are similar among mycobacterium species.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: tRNA modification patterns are similar among mycobacterium species.
source: tRNA modifying enzymes predicted in Mtb were observed in mycobacteria species, including Mycolicibacterium smegmatis and Mycobacteroides abscessus (Figure 1), suggesting that tRNA modification patterns are similar among mycobacterium species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of tRNA modifying enzymes across mycobacterial species.

claim: During cDNA synthesis, chemical modifications on tRNA nucleotides disrupt Watson–Crick base pairing and increase the frequency of reverse transcriptase errors, leading to incorporation of the incorrect nucleotide or early termination of cDNA synthesis.
source: During cDNA synthesis, chemical modifications on tRNA nucleotides disrupt Watson–Crick base pairing and increase the frequency of reverse transcriptase errors, leading to incorporation of the incorrect nucleotide or early termination of cDNA synthesis (Kellner et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Reverse transcription-derived 'signatures' typically correspond to modified sites.
source: These reverse transcription-derived 'signatures' typically correspond to modified sites (Zhang et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2015) and are depicted in the heatmap in Figure 2.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Comparison of the reverse transcription-derived signatures observed in Mtb to E. coli enables the prediction of the presence of common modifications, including ms2i6A, m1G, I, and k2C.
source: Comparison of the reverse transcription-derived signatures observed in Mtb to E. coli, where tRNA modifications have been well characterized (Kimura et al., 2020) enables the prediction of the presence of common modifications, including ms2i6A, m1G, I, and k2C (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of tRNA-seq data between Mtb and E. coli.

claim: These predictions are strongly supported by the set of tRNA modification enzymes identified in the Mtb genome, including miaA and miaB (ms2i6A), trmD (m1G), tadA (I), and tilS (k2C).
source: These predictions are strongly supported by the set of tRNA modification enzymes identified in the Mtb genome (Figure 1 and Supplementary file 3), including miaA and miaB (ms2i6A), trmD (m1G), tadA (I), and tilS (k2C).
evidence: This combines tRNA-seq data with homology search results to support the predictions.

claim: Some tRNA modifications were observed in Mtb but are not present in E. coli.
source: Some tRNA modifications were observed in Mtb but are not present in E. coli.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of tRNA-seq data.

claim: In other actinobacteria, A58 and A59 are likely modified to m1A.
source: In other actinobacteria, A58 and A59 are likely modified to m1A (Schwartz et al., 2018), and since trmI, the methylase that generates this modification is present in Mtb (Varshney et al., 2004), most Mtb tRNAs likely contain this modification as well.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Since trmI is present in Mtb, most Mtb tRNAs likely contain m1A modification at A58 and A59.
source: In other actinobacteria, A58 and A59 are likely modified to m1A (Schwartz et al., 2018), and since trmI, the methylase that generates this modification is present in Mtb (Varshney et al., 2004), most Mtb tRNAs likely contain this modification as well.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of trmI in Mtb and its known function.

claim: Nucleoside variation in the sequence of tRNA genes can account for some of the variations in modified sites between E. coli and Mtb.
source: Nucleoside variation in the sequence of tRNA genes can account for some of the variations in modified sites between E. coli and Mtb.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the basis for differences in modification patterns.

claim: In Mtb, termination signatures derived from G at position 37 were detected in tRNA-Arg2, -Gln1, and -Gln2.
source: For example, in Mtb, termination signatures derived from G at position 37 were detected in tRNA-Arg2, -Gln1, and -Gln2, whereas this position in these tRNAs in E. coli are modified A, such as m2A and m6A, which are silent in tRNA-seq.
evidence: This is based on the tRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Position 37 in tRNA-Arg2, -Gln1, and -Gln2 in E. coli are modified A, such as m2A and m6A, which are silent in tRNA-seq.
source: For example, in Mtb, termination signatures derived from G at position 37 were detected in tRNA-Arg2, -Gln1, and -Gln2, whereas this position in these tRNAs in E. coli are modified A, such as m2A and m6A, which are silent in tRNA-seq.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli tRNA modifications.

claim: Since m1G induces strong termination during reverse transcription, positions 37 in Mtb tRNA-Arg2, -Gln1, and -Gln2 are likely modified to m1G.
source: Since m1G induces strong termination during reverse transcription, these positions are likely modified to m1G, as observed in the Bacillus subtilis tRNA-Arg2 gene position 37 G (Jühling et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the RT signature and comparison to B. subtilis.

claim: m1G at position 37 G is observed in the Bacillus subtilis tRNA-Arg2 gene.
source: Since m1G induces strong termination during reverse transcription, these positions are likely modified to m1G, as observed in the Bacillus subtilis tRNA-Arg2 gene position 37 G (Jühling et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: IAA is a thiol-reactive compound that covalently attaches carboxyamidomethyl to thiolated uridines via nucleophilic substitution.
source: IAA is a thiol-reactive compound that covalently attaches carboxyamidomethyl to thiolated uridines via nucleophilic substitution (Herzog et al., 2017) and modified s4U is detected as C instead of U.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Modified s4U is detected as C instead of U after IAA treatment.
source: IAA is a thiol-reactive compound that covalently attaches carboxyamidomethyl to thiolated uridines via nucleophilic substitution (Herzog et al., 2017) and modified s4U is detected as C instead of U.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the effect of IAA treatment on s4U.

claim: In IAA-treated samples, positions 8 and 9, corresponding to s4U in many tRNA species, had high misincorporation frequencies.
source: In IAA-treated samples, positions 8 and 9, corresponding to s4U in many tRNA species, had high misincorporation frequencies, confirming that IAA treatment modifies s4U, leading to elevated misincorporation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the tRNA-seq data analysis of IAA-treated samples.

claim: IAA treatment modifies s4U, leading to elevated misincorporation.
source: In IAA-treated samples, positions 8 and 9, corresponding to s4U in many tRNA species, had high misincorporation frequencies, confirming that IAA treatment modifies s4U, leading to elevated misincorporation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is confirmed by the experimental data from IAA-treated tRNA-seq.

claim: Higher misincorporation and termination signals were observed at positions corresponding to other sulfur modifications, s2C, s2U and their derivatives, such as position 32 in tRNA-Arg3, -Arg5, -Ser3, and Arg4, and 34 in tRNA-Glu, -Gln1, and -Lys after IAA treatment.
source: Furthermore, we observed higher misincorporation and termination signals at the positions corresponding to other sulfur modification, s2C, s2U and their derivatives, such as position 32 in tRNA-Arg3, -Arg5, -Ser3, and Arg4, and 34 in tRNA-Glu, -Gln1, and -Lys (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), revealing that IAA treatment facilitates the detection of not only s4U but also additional sulfur modifications, which are weakly detected without the IAA treatment.
evidence: This is based on the tRNA-seq data analysis of IAA-treated samples.

claim: IAA treatment facilitates the detection of not only s4U but also additional sulfur modifications, which are weakly detected without the IAA treatment.
source: Furthermore, we observed higher misincorporation and termination signals at the positions corresponding to other sulfur modification, s2C, s2U and their derivatives, such as position 32 in tRNA-Arg3, -Arg5, -Ser3, and Arg4, and 34 in tRNA-Glu, -Gln1, and -Lys (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), revealing that IAA treatment facilitates the detection of not only s4U but also additional sulfur modifications, which are weakly detected without the IAA treatment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: IAA treatment increased termination signals from position 34 in tRNA-Glu1, -Gln1, and -Lys in Mtb.
source: IAA treatment increased termination signals from position 34 in tRNA-Glu1, -Gln1, and -Lys, which contain s2U derivatives in E. coli (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on the tRNA-seq data analysis of IAA-treated Mtb samples.

claim: Position 34 in tRNA-Glu1, -Gln1, and -Lys contain s2U derivatives in E. coli.
source: IAA treatment increased termination signals from position 34 in tRNA-Glu1, -Gln1, and -Lys, which contain s2U derivatives in E. coli (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli tRNA modifications.

claim: The 2-thiouridine modification is carried out by MnmA in E. coli.
source: The 2-thiouridine modification is carried out by MnmA in E. coli (Kambampati and Lauhon, 2003), and a homolog, Rv3024c, of this enzyme was identified in the Mtb genome (Supplementary file 3; Kapopoulou et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A homolog of E. coli MnmA, Rv3024c, was identified in the Mtb genome.
source: The 2-thiouridine modification is carried out by MnmA in E. coli (Kambampati and Lauhon, 2003), and a homolog, Rv3024c, of this enzyme was identified in the Mtb genome (Supplementary file 3; Kapopoulou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on the homology search results.

claim: Sequencing of tRNA isolated from MtbΔmnmA with prior IAA treatment showed reduced termination signals from position 34 in tRNA-Glu1, -Gln1, and -Lys in treated samples.
source: Sequencing of tRNA isolated from MtbΔmnmA with prior IAA treatment showed reduced termination signals from position 34 in tRNA-Glu1, -Gln1, and -Lys in treated samples, indicating that Rv3024c plays a critical role in the modification responsible for increased termination frequency derived from position 34 in these tRNAs (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is based on the tRNA-seq data analysis of the MtbΔmnmA mutant.

claim: Rv3024c plays a critical role in the modification responsible for increased termination frequency derived from position 34 in tRNA-Glu1, -Gln1, and -Lys.
source: Sequencing of tRNA isolated from MtbΔmnmA with prior IAA treatment showed reduced termination signals from position 34 in tRNA-Glu1, -Gln1, and -Lys in treated samples, indicating that Rv3024c plays a critical role in the modification responsible for increased termination frequency derived from position 34 in these tRNAs (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing WT and ΔmnmA strains.

claim: Rv3024c encodes an MnmA-like enzyme that sulfurates position 34 uridines in three Mtb tRNA isoacceptors.
source: Together, these observations strongly suggest that Rv3024c encodes an MnmA-like enzyme that sulfurates position 34 uridines in three Mtb tRNA isoacceptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined homology and experimental data.

claim: CMC treatment increased both misincorporation and termination signatures at a subset of Ψs in E. coli tRNAs.
source: As shown previously (Carlile et al., 2014), CMC treatment increased both misincorporation and termination signatures at a subset of Ψs in E. coli tRNAs (Figure 5, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
